objectives: Explain the difference between a class and an object
Write a class with fields, a method and a constructor
Predict what happens when two variables refer to the same object

exercises.prompt: Write a Book class with Title and Pages fields and a constructor that rejects a page count below 1. Then create two books.
exercises.answer: class Book { public string Title; public int Pages; public Book(string title, int pages) { if (pages < 1) throw new ArgumentException("Pages must be at least 1"); Title = title; Pages = pages; } } then var a = new Book("A", 100); var b = new Book("B", 250);. The class is written once; a and b are two objects with their own Title and Pages.

exercises.prompt: After `var x = new Book("A", 100); var y = x; y.Pages = 5;` what is x.Pages, and why?
exercises.answer: 5. Book is a class, so it is a reference type: `var y = x` copies the reference, not the object. x and y point to the same Book, so the change through y is visible through x. To get an independent copy you would have to create a new Book explicitly.

practical.title: Model a small thing as a class
practical.task: Pick something simple from daily life, such as a to-do item or a bank account. Write a class with two fields, one method and a constructor that rejects bad input, then create three objects and print them.
practical.done: The code runs, each object has its own values, and invalid input is rejected at creation.

objectives: Define an interface and implement it in two classes
Explain why code that depends on an interface is easier to change
Decide when an interface is not worth adding

exercises.prompt: Define an interface IShape with a method double Area(). Implement it in Circle and Square, then write a method that prints the total area of a list of shapes.
exercises.answer: interface IShape { double Area(); } class Circle : IShape { public double R; public double Area() => Math.PI * R * R; } class Square : IShape { public double Side; public double Area() => Side * Side; } double Total(IEnumerable<IShape> shapes) => shapes.Sum(s => s.Area()). Total never mentions Circle or Square, so a Triangle can be added later without changing it.

exercises.prompt: A teammate adds IUserRepository for a class that will only ever have one implementation and is never faked in tests. Is that a mistake?
exercises.answer: Mild over-engineering. An interface pays off when you need to swap implementations or substitute a fake. With neither, it adds a file and an indirection with no benefit. It is cheap to extract an interface later when a second implementation or a test need appears, so waiting is reasonable.

practical.title: Swap an implementation
practical.task: Write a small program that logs messages through an ILogger interface. Make a console logger and a fake in-memory logger, and use the fake to check what was logged.
practical.done: The same calling code works with both loggers, and you can assert on the in-memory messages.

objectives: Create a subclass that overrides a virtual method
Explain how one call can run different code for different objects
Judge whether a relationship is really is-a-kind-of

exercises.prompt: Create a base class Employee with a virtual method Pay() returning 1000. Make Manager override it to return base pay plus a 500 bonus. What do new Employee().Pay() and Employee e = new Manager(); e.Pay() return?
exercises.answer: The first returns 1000. The second returns 1500: the variable is typed Employee but the object is a Manager, and because Pay is virtual and overridden, dynamic dispatch runs the Manager version, which can call base.Pay() + 500.

exercises.prompt: Stack extends List so it can reuse Add and Remove. What is wrong with that choice?
exercises.answer: A stack is not a kind of list: it only allows adding and removing at one end. Inheriting exposes every List method, so callers can insert in the middle and break the stack's rule. Better to hold a private list inside (composition) and expose only Push, Pop and Peek.

practical.title: A small polymorphic program
practical.task: Make a base class Shape with a virtual Describe method and three subclasses that override it. Put one of each in a list typed as Shape and loop over it, calling Describe.
practical.done: The loop has no type checks, yet each shape prints its own description.

objectives: Judge whether a class is cohesive using the one-sentence test
Identify the concrete dependencies that make a class tightly coupled
Split a class that does too much into focused parts

exercises.prompt: A class InvoiceManager calculates tax, formats a PDF and writes to the database. Describe it in one sentence, and say how you would split it.
exercises.answer: "Calculates tax and formats a PDF and writes to the database" needs two ands, so cohesion is low. Split into TaxCalculator, InvoicePdfRenderer and IInvoiceStore. A small InvoiceService can then coordinate the three, and each part changes for only one reason.

exercises.prompt: List three signs that two classes are tightly coupled.
exercises.answer: A change in one forces edits in the other; one class reaches into the other's fields or internals; one class creates the other with new and needs its concrete type; tests of one cannot run without the other. Using an interface and passing the dependency in loosens all of these.

practical.title: Untangle a class
practical.task: Find a class that does more than one job. Write its one-sentence description, list its concrete dependencies, and split out one part behind an interface.
practical.done: Your description has no and, and one dependency is now injected and replaced by a fake in a test.

objectives: Say what invariant a class protects
Choose composition over inheritance and explain the trade-off
Avoid constructor traps such as calling virtual methods

exercises.prompt: A class has private fields, each with a public getter and setter. Is it encapsulated? Explain using an example of an invariant.
exercises.answer: Not meaningfully. Encapsulation is about protecting invariants, not hiding fields. If an Order exposes SetTotal, callers can make the total disagree with the line items. A better design exposes AddLine and computes the total internally, so the object can never reach an invalid state.

exercises.prompt: Why is calling a virtual method from a base class constructor dangerous?
exercises.answer: The derived override runs before the derived constructor has initialised its own state, so it can see nulls or default values. In C# and Java the override really does run at that point. C++ dispatches to the base version during construction, which surprises people differently.

practical.title: Replace inheritance in real code
practical.task: Find a class in a project you work on that inherits mainly to reuse code. Sketch or make the change to composition: inject the collaborator and delegate to it.
practical.done: You can name what got easier to test or change, and anything that got worse.

objectives: Distinguish dependency inversion from dependency injection
Pick the right service lifetime and spot captive dependencies
Explain how a hierarchical injector resolves a token

exercises.prompt: In ASP.NET Core, a singleton service takes a scoped DbContext in its constructor. What goes wrong?
exercises.answer: This is a captive dependency. The singleton holds one DbContext for the application's lifetime, so a context meant for one request is shared across requests, is not thread-safe and accumulates tracked entities. Validation catches this in development by default. The fix is to inject IServiceScopeFactory and create a scope for each unit of work.

exercises.prompt: What's the difference between dependency inversion and dependency injection? Can you have one without the other?
exercises.answer: Dependency inversion is a design principle: high-level code depends on abstractions, not on details. Dependency injection is a mechanism: a dependency is supplied from outside. You can inject a concrete class, which is injection without inversion. You can also invert with a hand-written factory or by passing a function, with no container involved.

practical.title: Make a hard-to-test class testable
practical.task: Find code that calls the clock, a database or an HTTP client directly. Inject that dependency and write one test using a fake, for example a fixed clock.
practical.done: A test that was impossible or flaky before now runs fast and gives the same result each time.

objectives: Diagnose which principle is violated from a symptom
Explain Liskov substitution in terms of behaviour
Avoid over-engineering in the name of open/closed

exercises.prompt: Square inherits from Rectangle and overrides SetWidth to also set the height. Which principle does this break? Show the calling code that fails.
exercises.answer: Liskov substitution. Code that uses a Rectangle can reasonably expect: r.SetWidth(5); r.SetHeight(4); then r.Area() == 20. With a Square the area is 16. The subtype compiles, but it breaks the behaviour its base type promised.

exercises.prompt: A switch on payment type appears in five places, and each new payment type means editing all five. Which principle helps, and when would adding an abstraction be premature?
exercises.answer: Open/closed: put the behaviour behind an interface, with one implementation per payment type, so a new type means a new class. It's premature when there's one switch, two stable cases and no sign of change. A simple conditional is cheaper until real variation appears.

practical.title: Audit a class from your codebase
practical.task: Take the largest service class in a project you know. List its reasons to change and its dependencies, then name one concrete split that would remove a reason to change.
practical.done: You have a short written note naming the principle, the symptom and the split, and you've judged whether it's worth doing now.

objectives: Choose a pattern from the problem, not from its name
Tell look-alike patterns apart by intent
Recognise when a pattern adds more than it saves

exercises.prompt: Decorator, Proxy and Adapter all wrap an object. How do you tell them apart?
exercises.answer: By intent. Adapter changes the interface so an incompatible class fits. Decorator keeps the interface and adds behaviour, and decorators can stack. Proxy keeps the interface and controls access, for example lazy loading, caching or permission checks.

exercises.prompt: Strategy and Chain of Responsibility both select behaviour at runtime. What's the structural difference, and when does each fit?
exercises.answer: With Strategy, the caller or context picks exactly one algorithm behind an interface, which fits interchangeable algorithms like pricing rules. With a chain, the request passes through handlers that can each process it, pass it on or stop it, which fits middleware and approval flows.

practical.title: Find a pattern you already use
practical.task: Open your framework's middleware or HTTP pipeline, such as ASP.NET Core middleware or Angular interceptors. Identify the pattern it uses and write a small custom link in that chain.
practical.done: Your custom link runs in the real pipeline, and you can say why this pattern fits better than a Strategy here.
